one_liner: KVM-based userspace sandbox that resets a forked Linux program in tens of microseconds, versus milliseconds for process fork or V8 isolates.
what_it_does: A C++ library that loads an ordinary static or dynamic x86-64 Linux ELF into a minimal KVM guest, emulates the Linux syscalls it needs on the host side, and lets the host call guest functions (vmcall/timed_vmcall) with timeouts and memory limits. A master VM is run to an initialised state, prepare_copy_on_write() freezes it, and cheap forks (Machine{master, options}) serve work and are rewound with reset_to(master). The API is an embedding interface, not a drop-in for fork() or an isolate: libriscv/kvmserver and Varnish's VMOD-TinyKVM wrap it to serve unmodified server binaries one request per VM.
how_it_is_fast: Guest code runs directly on the CPU under hardware virtualization, so compute (including JIT-compiled code such as V8 inside Deno) runs at native speed; only syscalls that need the host exit the VM (about 1 us each per kvmserver). Forks share the master's memory copy-on-write: write faults allocate pages from per-fork memory banks and record them in a sorted dirty-page list, and reset_to() restores just those pages and the registers instead of tearing down an address space, so reset cost scales with pages written (68 KB to 2.3 MB per request in kvmserver's examples). Page copies use AVX2 loads and stores on x86-64, and hugepage-backed loading is optional.
when_to_use: Per-request isolation of a JIT runtime (Deno/V8, LuaJIT-style engines) or native server where Wasm would cost the JIT and fork or isolate creation costs milliseconds; kvmserver's React page renders in 695 us with a fresh VM per request against 646 us native.
Multi-tenant edge or HTTP-cache workloads that must wipe all guest memory between requests and bound each call with a timeout and memory limit.
Running prebuilt Linux x86-64 binaries in a sandbox without a cross toolchain or recompilation, on hosts that expose /dev/kvm.
Large initialised programs (tens to hundreds of MB RSS) forked many times, since forks only allocate pages they write.
when_not_to_use: Tiny handlers where a few tens of microseconds matter: per request it is slower than native (Rust minimal server 13 us native vs 28 us ephemeral, Deno hello world 17 vs 50 us).
Hosts without /dev/kvm or inside nested virtualization (kvmserver measured about 200 us extra per request nested under QEMU), or non-Linux hosts.

Multithreaded guests: kvmserver says threads should be avoided and parallelism comes from forking VMs; aarch64 has no SMP, no remote VMs, no dynamic ELF loading tested and no published performance numbers.
Projects that cannot accept GPL-3.0 (the alternative is a commercial licence from Varnish Software; contributions need a CLA).

Hostile multi-tenant deployments that assume the isolation is mature: August 2026 fixes closed a host out-of-bounds read (#98), reset_to() leaking signal handlers, cwd, brk and pipe flags across requests (#103), and several syscall-policy bypasses (#94, #95).

integration.dependencies: Linux KVM (/dev/kvm), pthread, rt; kvmserver adds CLI11
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 hosts with AVX2 (page copies call avx2_page_duplicate with no runtime CPU check); Linux aarch64 backend partial (static ELF, 4 KiB pages, no SMP)
integration.thread_safety: One Machine per thread; forks of one master can run in parallel on separate threads (the pooled benchmark keeps one fork per worker thread). Errors are reported with C++ exceptions (MachineException).

gotchas: No benchmark in this repo is published: all per-request numbers are from libriscv/kvmserver (Ryzen 9 7950X, Deno 2.3.6, build flags not stated). Its README tables have fewer rows than the current examples/bench.ts produces, so they come from an earlier harness, and kvmserver pins a TinyKVM from 2026-03-06, before the August 2026 reset and sandbox fixes. The 1.5-2 orders-of-magnitude claim over fork, V8 isolates and Wasm rests on unpublished 'previous experiments'.

Harness: in kvmserver's bench.ts the Wasmtime serve and Node isolated-vm groups use TCP to 127.0.0.1:8000 with keep-alive and 100 warm-up requests, while the kvmserver ephemeral rows use a Unix socket, a new connection per request and 1000 warm-ups, so a rerun of those groups is not like-for-like. The 'no-tail' row (2 VMs, 1 connection) hides the reset on the idle VM, so its 639 us React figure is latency with the reset off the critical path, not a win over native.

Harness: TinyKVM's own src/bench.cpp times fork, vmcall and reset with CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID, which leaves out time the thread is blocked; the repo's snapshot_bench.cpp says so and switches to CLOCK_MONOTONIC. bench.cpp's 'vmcall + destructor' line also includes the fork loop and warm-up calls, and benchmark_multiple_vms frees its placement-new Machines without destroying them, leaking VMs into later runs.

Resetting a fork to a different master (allow_reset_to_new_master) comes 'at a steep cost', and alternating VMs on one thread carries a 'serious penalty on Linux' (bench.cpp comments); reset time also grows with open file descriptors and dirty pages.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick TinyKVM over Wasm engines such as WAMR, or pre-initialisation with Wizer, when the guest is an existing native or JIT-compiled Linux binary that must keep its JIT and get a fresh state every request. Pick LFI when you can recompile and want in-process isolation at about 7% overhead without KVM, and a Wasm runtime when you need portability beyond Linux/KVM.
verified_claims_summary: libriscv/kvmserver, built on TinyKVM, measured with oha on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (Deno 2.3.6 with --v8-flags=--predictable, 1000 warm-up requests, build flags not stated): React page rendering 646 us native vs 695 us with a fresh VM per request (about 80 us overhead, 55 us of it reset), Rust minimal server 13 vs 28 us, Deno hello world 17 vs 50 us. The only baseline in the tables is native, which wins; the claimed win over process fork, V8 isolates and Wasmtime has no published numbers.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-08-21, 823 stars, recent fuzzing and security hardening by Varnish maintainers) and used in VMOD-TinyKVM and kvmserver, but GPL-3.0 or commercial only and still fixing isolation bugs, so audit before trusting it with hostile tenants.
